## Why compress a dotplot? {#purpose-18}

Imagine **nine workshop students** whose one-way travel times, in minutes, are **5, 8, 10, 12, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18**. A dotplot retains each time. A boxplot makes it easier to compare a few important numerical landmarks, though it loses some detail.

**Before calculating:** predict which values bracket approximately the middle half of the nine journeys. What happens to the box if we change only the largest time?

## 1 · The five-number summary {#five-18}

**Sort the data first.** Record the *minimum*, *first quartile* ($Q_1$), *median*, *third quartile* ($Q_3$), and *maximum* **in that order**:

$$
(\text{minimum},\ Q_1,\ \text{median},\ Q_3,\ \text{maximum}).
$$

The middle observation of our nine sorted travel times is the **fifth**, 12 minutes, so the median is 12. We use the *median-of-halves* convention from [Topic 1.7](<../Topic 1.7/topic-1-7.qmd>): for odd sample sizes, **exclude the overall median** when forming the two halves. The lower half **5, 8, 10, 12** has quartile $Q_1=(8+10)/2=9$ minutes. The upper half **14, 15, 16, 18** has $Q_3=(15+16)/2=15.5$ minutes. Therefore,

$$
\boxed{(5,\ 9,\ 12,\ 15.5,\ 18)\ \text{minutes}}.
$$

A numerical five-number summary should identify the **measured variable** and its **units**. These summaries describe the nine travel times in the sample.

<details class="math-note"><summary>Why these five numbers? — A convention, not a theorem</summary>
<p>The extremes locate the endpoints, and the three quartiles divide an ordered sample into approximately four equal-count portions. Some software uses interpolation or includes the overall median in both halves. These definitions may disagree for small samples. <strong>No universal mathematical proof selects one quartile convention.</strong> State the method and apply it consistently to the table, graph, and worked solutions.</p>
</details>

The **interquartile range (IQR)** is the length of the interval occupied by the middle half:

$$
IQR=Q_3-Q_1=15.5-9=\boxed{6.5\text{ minutes}}.
$$

This is a difference in **minutes**, not the number of students between the quartiles. It is a measure of *spread* (introduced in Topic 1.7), whereas the median measures *center*.

<details class="math-note"><summary>Why subtract the quartiles? — Definition and interpretation</summary>
<p>The length of any numerical interval from a to b is b−a. Because the box extends from Q1 to Q3, its numerical width equals Q3−Q1 by definition. This middle-half spread is usually less affected by changing an extreme observation than a range or standard deviation. It is a <strong>definition</strong>, not a universal claim that all datasets contain exactly half their distinct values between the quartiles.</p>
</details>

### Quick checkpoint

Suppose the sorted data are **2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, 13**. The overall median is **7**. Excluding it, the lower triple has median **4** and upper triple has median **10**. The summary is **(2, 4, 7, 10, 13)**, not (2, 5, 7, 9, 13). When you form quartiles, do not confuse the half boundaries with the middle observation of each half.
